title: How to Make Good Habits Easy and Bad Habits Hard
author: Elevated Path
summary: Elevated Path argues that most people misdiagnose their inconsistency as a discipline problem when it's actually an environment-design problem. Drawing on the concept of 'activation energy,' the piece reframes habit formation around reducing the number of steps between intention and action for desired behaviors, while deliberately adding friction to unwanted ones. Rather than urging more willpower, the author offers five concrete practices: identify the habit you keep planning but not doing, prepare tomorrow's first action before ending today, make good habits visually unavoidable, make bad habits mildly annoying to access, and reset your environment nightly for your future self. The piece leans on Thaler and Sunstein's 'choice architecture' to frame this as a deliberate design exercise rather than a personality trait, closing with the reassurance that a 'disciplined' identity is built through small environmental decisions rather than found through sheer willpower.
points: The core reframe — 'you don't have a discipline problem, you have a habit of making the wrong thing easier' — shifts the locus of change from willpower to environment design, which is the article's most memorable and actionable claim.
Practical diagnostic: instead of asking 'how do I force myself to do this,' ask 'what happens in the five minutes before I actually do this' to locate exactly where friction is hiding.

The 'prepare the next action before you finish the current one' practice (clearing the desk, writing tomorrow's first task) is framed as 'proactive laziness' — a reusable, low-effort ritual leaders can apply to their own routines or recommend to teams.

Borrowing Thaler and Sunstein's 'choice architecture,' the piece treats habit design as an active decision about what gets the 'express lane' versus the 'speed bump,' rather than a passive hope for more self-control.
quotes: You think you have a discipline problem. You probably don't. You have a habit of making the wrong thing easier.
There is always a gap between: "I should do this." and "I am doing this." That gap is friction.
Instead of asking: "How do I force myself to do this?" Ask: "Why is this harder to start than it needs to be?
You're making a decision today that your future self won't have to make. That's proactive laziness. And honestly? That's a good thing.
Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein call this broader idea choice architecture: the way choices are arranged can influence what people actually choose.
Your environment doesn't care about your goals. It will make whatever is convenient easier. So make convenience work for you.
The disciplined version of you wasn't hiding somewhere inside you waiting to emerge. You built them. One tiny environmental decision at a time.
